characters: Zulaiha: a thoughtful eight-year-old Ghanaian girl wearing a neat green-and-yellow school uniform and a cream headscarf.
Nsoh: her lively eight-year-old male classmate with short neat hair, wearing a matching yellow uniform shirt and green shorts.
Their teacher: a kind Ghanaian woman wearing a warm coral-and-gold African-print dress.

narrationPlan.voice: A thoughtful girl’s voice for Zulaiha; a lively voice for Nsoh
narrationPlan.pace: Patient, with a pause for waiting (about 90 words per minute)
notes: Read dialogue with a different voice for each character.
Pause for two seconds at each question activity.
Never rush the last page: let the ending land.

music: A slow, rising flute, like something climbing (placeholder)
culturalNotes: School gardens are common across Ghanaian primary schools. Pale-petalled flowers, soft leafy stems, or celery stalks show coloured water transport clearly.
Use safe food colouring only, have the teacher handle any cutting tool, and wash hands afterwards.
reviewQuestions: Is the language right for the stated age band and reading level?
Is anything here inaccurate, stereotyped or unsafe for children?
Check that locally available white flowers or pale leafy stems show colour uptake within several hours to overnight.
Confirm the explanation (roots absorb water; narrow tubes in the stem transport it upward) with the Integrated Science syllabus.

teacherGuide.overview: A hands-on observation showing coloured water travelling up a plant stem. Learners discover the roles of roots and stems, practise patient observation over time, and apply smart garden watering.
learningGoals: State what roots and stems do for a plant.
Predict and observe gradual change over several hours.
Explain why gardeners water the soil around the roots.

subjectLinks.subject: Integrated Science
subjectLinks.link: Parts of a plant and their functions

beforeReading: Ask: how can a tall plant drink water when it has no mouth?
whileReading: Pause on page 3 and ask learners what they predict the flower will look like the next morning.
afterReading: Place a pale flower or leafy stalk into safe coloured water and draw it after one hour and again the next day.
Draw a simple plant and point to its roots, stem, leaves, and flower.
discussion: Why should we pour water at the base of a plant instead of splashing the leaves?
How can we conserve water in the school garden?
reflection: What did you observe carefully today by being patient?

support: Compare two jars side by side—one with red water and one with plain clear water.
stretch: Predict what happens when a teacher splits the lower stem lengthways into two cups of different food colours.

culturalNotes: School gardens are common across Ghanaian primary schools. Pale-petalled flowers, soft leafy stems, or celery stalks show coloured water transport clearly.
Use safe food colouring only, have the teacher handle any cutting tool, and wash hands afterwards.
localiseThis: Use safe non-toxic plants and pale blossoms growing near the school.
Ensure only the teacher trims stems and all pupils wash hands with soap afterwards.

factCheck.claim: Plant roots absorb water from soil and tiny tubes (xylem vessels) inside the stem carry it up to leaves and petals.
factCheck.explanation: Water moves upward through narrow transport tubes in the stem via transpiration pull and capillary action, which becomes visible when safe food dye tints pale petals.
